With plotnine, you choose the data, say which columns control position,
colour or size, and add layers that draw points, lines or bars.

## Your first plot

Click Run below a code block to try it. Edit the exercise code and run it
again to see what changes.

We'll use [Gapminder](https://www.gapminder.org/) data on life expectancy,
population and GDP per person in African countries in 2007. GDP per
person is a measure of economic output per person.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_0
#| caption: ""
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_2007 = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa_2007.csv")
africa_2007.head()
```

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [gap_1, gap_2, gap_3, gap_4]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_2007 = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa_2007.csv")
```

Start with `ggplot()`. Give it the data and use `aes()` to say which
columns control the visual properties. Add `geom_point()` to draw a
point for each row.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_1
#| caption: ""
#| autorun: true
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point()
)
```

`gdpPercap` controls horizontal position; `lifeExp` controls vertical
position. Each point represents a country.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Swap `x` and `y` and run the code again. The data is the same; only the
mapping changed.
:::

## More mappings

We can also use colour to show which region each country belongs to:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_2
#| caption: ""
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color="region"))
)
```

Mappings can go in `ggplot()`, where every layer uses them, or in a
layer's own `aes()`, where only that layer uses them.

Use population (`pop`) to control point size:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_3
#| caption: ""
#| autorun: true
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color="region", size="pop"))
)
```

::: {.task}
Now use colour to show life expectancy. Replace the blank with
`"lifeExp"`:
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_4
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color=___), size=3)
)
```

::: {.solution exercise="gap_4"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: gap_4
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(africa_2007, aes(x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_point(aes(color="lifeExp"), size=3)
)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What changed?

Compare the colour legend with the one for `region`. Why is it different?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

`region` contains category labels, so each region gets a distinct colour.
`lifeExp` contains numbers, so the colours change gradually from low to
high values.

Inside `aes()`, colour or size comes from a data column. Outside `aes()`,
it is a fixed setting. Here, `size=3` makes every point the same size.
:::

## Layers

Next, we'll look at life expectancy over time in East Africa:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_0
#| caption: ""
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_history = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")
ea_countries = ["Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda"]
east_africa = africa_history.query("country in @ea_countries")
east_africa.head()
```

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [layers_1, layers_2, parsons, facet_1]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_history = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")
east_africa = africa_history[
    africa_history.country.isin(["Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda"])
]
```

Let's draw a line through the points:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_1
#| caption: ""
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line()
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What went wrong?

We wanted a separate line for each country. What is missing?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

We haven't told plotnine which points belong together. It draws one line
through all the countries, connecting points in order of year.
:::

::: {.task}
Use `group` to draw a line for each country. Then add points coloured
by country.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_2
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group=___), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="layers_2"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Each line is one country.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="layers_2"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: layers_2
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
)
```
:::
:::

Layers are drawn in the order you add them, so the points sit on top of
the lines. Swap the two layers and run it again to see the difference.

Rwanda's line falls sharply around the time of the 1994 genocide, then
rises again.

## Put it in order

::: {.task}
Rearrange the code to reproduce the plot below. Remove the line you
don't need. You can cut and paste within the editor.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

africa_history = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_africa.csv")
east_africa = africa_history[
    africa_history.country.isin(["Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania", "Uganda"])
]
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
    + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="Country")
)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: parsons
    + facet_wrap("region")
    + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="Country")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
)
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
(
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
```

::: {.hint exercise="parsons"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Start with `ggplot()`, then add the lines and points in drawing order.
The example has one panel.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="parsons"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: parsons
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(east_africa, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="country"))
    + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="Country")
)
```
:::
:::

## Separate panels

Putting every country in one plot makes the lines hard to follow.
`facet_wrap()` gives each region its own panel. These separate views are
called *facets*.

::: {.task}
Remove `+ facet_wrap("region")` to see all the lines together.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: facet_1
#| autorun: true
(
    ggplot(africa_history, aes(x="year", y="lifeExp"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="country"), color="grey")
    + facet_wrap("region")
)
```

Here, `region` decides which panel each country appears in.

::: {.callout-important}
## What do you see?

Which region has a pattern that was hard to see with all the lines together?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

In Southern Africa, life expectancy rose, then fell sharply during the
HIV/AIDS epidemic. Separating the regions makes that pattern easier to
see.
:::

## The census data

Let's return to the census table. Its tidy rows made the figures look
plausible. To notice the problem, you had to compare populations across
the two years.

We'll plot those pairs of values to make the change easier to see.

### The data

`census_long.csv` holds each tribe's population in the 2014 and 2024
censuses, in two versions: `bad` (the provisional report) and `good` (the
corrected final report).

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_0
#| caption: ""
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

census = pd.read_csv("data/census_long.csv")

# Use the corrected populations to keep tribe order the same in both panels
tribe_order = (
    census.query("version == 'good' and year == 2024")
    .sort_values("population")
    .tribe
)
census["tribe"] = pd.Categorical(census.tribe, categories=tribe_order)

# Treat years as categories so each census gets a distinct colour
census["year"] = census.year.astype(str)

# Leave out "Other tribes" so the smaller populations are easier to compare
census = census[census.tribe != "Other tribes"]

provisional = census[census.version == "bad"]
provisional.head()
```

The setup makes two choices for this plot:

- Treat the years as text so each census gets a distinct colour.
- Leave out "Other tribes" so its large population doesn't compress the
  rest of the plot. We'll keep that row in the tables.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [census_1, census_2, census_3]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

census = pd.read_csv("data/census_long.csv")
tribe_order = (
    census.query("version == 'good' and year == 2024")
    .sort_values("population")
    .tribe
)
census["tribe"] = pd.Categorical(census.tribe, categories=tribe_order)
census["year"] = census.year.astype(str)
census = census[census.tribe != "Other tribes"]
provisional = census[census.version == "bad"]
```

### Points and lines

::: {.task}
Use `population` for horizontal position, `tribe` for vertical position
and `year` for colour. Group by tribe to join its two points with a line.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_1
(
    ggplot(provisional, aes(x=___, y=___))
    + geom_line(aes(group=___), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color=___), size=3)
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="census_1"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Column names go in quotes: `x="population"`. Each line joins the two
points for one tribe.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="census_1"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_1
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(provisional, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
)
```
:::
:::

Add the line layer first so the points appear on top of it.

::: {.callout-important}
## What do you see?

The population across these tribes grew by about a quarter between
2014 and 2024. Which lines suggest a fall or unusually large rise?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Bagisu and Acholi appear to shrink while the country's population grew.
Bakiga and Langi appear to grow much faster than tribes of similar size.

These four tribes had their 2014 figures swapped with each other.
:::

### The corrected figures

::: {.task}
Now plot both versions side by side. `census` holds the `bad` and `good`
rows; split them into panels with `facet_wrap()`.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_2
(
    ggplot(census, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
    + facet_wrap(___)
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="census_2"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Which column says whether a row is from the provisional or the corrected
report?
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="census_2"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_2
#| solution: true
(
    ggplot(census, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
    + facet_wrap("version")
)
```
:::
:::

In the corrected figures every tribe grows, and by similar proportions.

### A closer look (optional)

If time allows, compare the smaller tribes in the two panels. Can you
find any other figures that changed? Use the plot below as a starting
point and edit it as you like.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: census_3
#| caption: ""
small_tribes = ["Lugbara", "Banyoro", "Alur", "Bakonzo", "Batoro", "Bafumbira"]
small = census.query("tribe in @small_tribes")

(
    ggplot(small, aes(x="population", y="tribe"))
    + geom_line(aes(group="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point(aes(color="year"), size=3)
    + facet_wrap("version")
    + scale_x_continuous(labels=lambda s: [f"{x/1e6:.1f}M" for x in s])
)
```

The last line labels the axis in millions. It changes how the numbers
are written; the points stay in the same positions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Banyoro, Alur and Bakonzo also had their 2014 figures swapped. Banyoro
got Alur's figure, Alur got Bakonzo's and Bakonzo got Banyoro's. Their
populations are close in size, so these swaps are harder to notice.
:::

### The change in view

In the table, you had to read and compare two numbers to see the change.
In the plot, each point shows a population and the line between them
shows how much it changed. A backwards or unusually long line draws your
attention to figures worth checking.

## Other views of growth

The paired points joined by lines form a *dumbbell chart*. Below are
other ways to show the same data. Run the examples and try changing them.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [alt_bars, alt_box, alt_lollipop, alt_index]
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

census = pd.read_csv("data/census_long.csv")
census = census[census.tribe != "Other tribes"]
tribe_order = (
    census.query("version == 'good' and year == 2024")
    .sort_values("population")
    .tribe
)
census["tribe"] = pd.Categorical(census.tribe, categories=tribe_order)

# One row per tribe and version, with the growth between the two censuses
wide = census.pivot_table(
    index=["tribe", "version"],
    columns="year",
    values="population",
    observed=True,
).reset_index()
wide.columns = ["tribe", "version", "pop_2014", "pop_2024"]
wide["growth"] = (wide.pop_2024 / wide.pop_2014 - 1) * 100

# Compare each tribe with the median growth in its own report
wide["vs_typical"] = wide.growth - wide.groupby("version").growth.transform("median")
```

### Bar chart of growth

Each bar shows growth from zero. Sorting puts falls at the bottom and
the largest rises at the top. The dashed line marks the median, the
middle growth value when the tribes are sorted.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_bars
#| caption: ""
provisional = wide[wide.version == "bad"].sort_values("growth")
provisional = provisional.assign(
    tribe=pd.Categorical(provisional.tribe.astype(str), categories=provisional.tribe.astype(str))
)
median_growth = provisional.growth.median()

(
    ggplot(provisional, aes(x="tribe", y="growth"))
    + geom_col()
    + annotate("hline", yintercept=median_growth, linetype="dashed")
    + annotate("text", label="median", x=1, y=median_growth, ha="left")
    + coord_flip()
    + labs(y="Growth, 2014 to 2024 (%)")
)
```

### Box plot of growth

A box plot summarises how growth varies within each report. The box
contains the middle half of the values. The labelled points show tribes
whose growth is far from the median.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_box
#| caption: ""
outliers = wide[wide.vs_typical.abs() > 15]

(
    ggplot(wide, aes(x="version", y="growth"))
    + geom_boxplot(outlier_alpha=0)
    + geom_point()
    + geom_text(aes(label="tribe"), data=outliers, ha="left", nudge_x=0.08, size=8)
    + labs(y="Growth, 2014 to 2024 (%)")
)
```

### Lollipop chart of growth

Each point shows a tribe's growth, with a line back to zero. The panels
let you compare the provisional and corrected figures.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_lollipop
#| caption: ""
(
    ggplot(wide, aes(x="growth", y="tribe"))
    + geom_segment(aes(x=0, xend="growth", yend="tribe"), color="grey")
    + geom_point()
    + facet_wrap("version")
    + labs(x="Growth, 2014 to 2024 (%)")
)
```

### Growth from a shared starting point

Each tribe starts at 1, representing its population in 2014. The second
point shows its 2024 population relative to that starting value. Ending
at 2 means doubling; ending below 1 means shrinking. This lets us
compare growth across tribes of different sizes.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: alt_index
#| caption: ""
provisional = wide[wide.version == "bad"]
index = provisional.melt(
    id_vars=["tribe", "growth", "vs_typical"],
    value_vars=["pop_2014", "pop_2024"],
    var_name="year",
    value_name="population",
).assign(
    year=lambda d: d.year.str[-4:],
    population=lambda d: d.population / d.groupby("tribe").population.transform("first"),
    shrank=lambda d: d.growth < 0,
)

(
    ggplot(index, aes(x="year", y="population", group="tribe", color="shrank"))
    + geom_line()
    + geom_point()
    + geom_text(
        aes(label="tribe"),
        data=index[(index.year == "2024") & (index.vs_typical.abs() > 15)],
        ha="left",
        nudge_x=0.05,
        size=8,
    )
    + annotate("hline", yintercept=1)
    + annotate("text", label="No Growth", x=float("inf"), y=1, va="bottom", ha="right", size=8)
    + scale_x_discrete(expand=(0.05, 0, 0.4, 0))
    + labs(y="Population (2014 = 1)")
    + theme(legend_position="none")
)
```

Each plot makes the unusual growth visible in a different way. Which
one would you choose for someone checking the census figures?
